---
title: "Eigenmodes of a recurrent network"
description: "Why a linear network is easier to read in the basis of its eigenvectors: every mode decays or grows at its own rate, and the slowest one is the one that lasts."
toc: true
execute:
  enabled: false
---

A network of neurons that feed back on each other can do something a single
neuron cannot: it can hold on to its activity. A single neuron forgets its
input within a membrane time constant, a few tens of milliseconds. Cortical
areas, by contrast, show fluctuations that last hundreds of milliseconds or
seconds, and the duration grows along the cortical hierarchy (Murray et al.
2014). The simplest explanation is recurrence. Activity that excites the
neurons that excite it back can outlive any single cell, and how long it
lasts depends on how strong the loop is.

The trick is to stop looking at the activity neuron by neuron and look at it mode by mode, where the modes
are the eigenvectors of the connection matrix. I wrote this up as an
exercise when I was a teaching assistant for the *Theoretical Neuroscience*
lecture at Goethe University Frankfurt.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = ({size: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize, family: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily, toString() { return this.size + " " + this.family; }})
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## The model

The network has $N$ neurons with firing rates collected in a vector $r$. Each
neuron relaxes towards its input with time constant $\tau$, and its input is
the sum of an external drive $h$ and what it receives from the other neurons
through the $N \times N$ connection matrix $\mathbf M$:

$$\tau \frac{dr}{dt} = -r + \mathbf M r + h .$$

There is no nonlinearity, which is a real restriction, but it is what makes
the following exact. If $\mathbf M$ is real and symmetric, it has $N$
orthogonal eigenvectors $v_i$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$, so that
$\mathbf M v_i = \lambda_i v_i$. Any
activity pattern can be written as a weighted sum of these eigenvectors,
$r = \sum_i a_i v_i$, and the weights $a_i$ are found by projecting,
$a_i = v_i^{\mathsf T} r$. Substituting into the equation and projecting onto
each $v_i$ in turn gives $N$ separate equations, one per mode:

$$\tau \frac{da_i}{dt} = -(1 - \lambda_i)\, a_i + h_i ,$$

where $h_i = v_i^{\mathsf T} h$ is the part of the input that lies along mode
$i$. The modes do not talk to each other. Each one is a leaky integrator on
its own, with an effective time constant

$$\tau_i = \frac{\tau}{1 - \lambda_i}$$

and a steady state $a_i^\ast = h_i / (1 - \lambda_i)$. A mode whose
eigenvalue is close to 1 is slow and amplifies its input strongly. A mode
with a negative eigenvalue is faster than a single neuron and suppresses its
input. If any eigenvalue exceeds 1 the corresponding mode grows without
bound, which is where the linear model stops being useful and the
[recurrent networks page](recurrent-networks.qmd) takes over.

The smallest example makes this concrete. Two neurons that excite each other
with weight $w$ have $\mathbf M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & w \\ w & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, with
eigenvectors $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$ and eigenvalues $w$ and
$-w$. The common mode, both neurons active together, decays with time
constant $\tau/(1 - w)$, slower than a single neuron. The difference mode,
one up and one down, decays with $\tau/(1 + w)$, faster. Start the pair in
any state and the difference dies away first, leaving both neurons at the
same level. Everything on this page is that example with more neurons.

The figure uses $N = 40$ neurons and a random symmetric matrix with
independent Gaussian entries, scaled so that its largest eigenvalue is a
number $R$ you control. $R$ is often called the spectral bound. The remaining
eigenvalues spread out below $R$, roughly symmetrically about zero, so the
network has one slow mode and many fast ones. For a large matrix of this
kind the eigenvalues fill a semicircle, Wigner's semicircle law (Wigner
1958), and with 40 neurons the bottom panel shows a rough version of it.
Pachitariu et al. (2026) argue that the activity of the mouse brain looks much like
such a random symmetric network sitting close to the stability limit, which
is the regime at the top of the $R$ slider. David Dahmen and colleagues
reach a related conclusion from the other direction: Dahmen et al. (2019)
show that the weak average correlations in motor cortex are what a strongly
recurrent network close to that limit produces, and Dahmen et al. (2026) find
that the strength of local recurrence sets how many dimensions the activity
of a cortical area occupies. In the language of this page, the closer $R$ is
to 1, the fewer modes carry the activity.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof emR = Inputs.range([0, 0.98], {value: 0.9, step: 0.01, label: "Spectral bound R (largest eigenvalue)"})
viewof emStart = Inputs.radio(new Map([["random pattern", "random"], ["slowest mode", "slow"], ["fastest mode", "fast"], ["slowest + fastest", "both"]]), {value: "random", label: "Initial activity"})
viewof emDrive = Inputs.radio(new Map([["none, activity decays", "none"], ["constant random input", "const"]]), {value: "none", label: "Input h"})
viewof emNoise = Inputs.range([0, 0.2], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "Input noise"})
viewof emNew = Inputs.button("New random network")
viewof emPause = Inputs.toggle({label: "Pause"})
viewof emReset = Inputs.button("Reset")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
emN = 40
emRandn = () => {
  let u = 0; while (u === 0) u = Math.random();
  return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * Math.random());
}
// Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm for a symmetric matrix; returns eigenvalues sorted descending with eigenvectors as rows
emEigh = A0 => {
  const n = A0.length, A = A0.map(row => Float64Array.from(row));
  const V = Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => { const r = new Float64Array(n); r[i] = 1; return r; });
  for (let sweep = 0; sweep < 60; sweep++) {
    let off = 0; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) off += A[i][j] * A[i][j];
    if (off < 1e-20) break;
    for (let p = 0; p < n; p++) for (let q = p + 1; q < n; q++) {
      if (Math.abs(A[p][q]) < 1e-14) continue;
      const theta = (A[q][q] - A[p][p]) / (2 * A[p][q]);
      const t = Math.sign(theta || 1) / (Math.abs(theta) + Math.sqrt(theta * theta + 1));
      const c = 1 / Math.sqrt(t * t + 1), s = t * c;
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const akp = A[k][p], akq = A[k][q]; A[k][p] = c * akp - s * akq; A[k][q] = s * akp + c * akq; }
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const apk = A[p][k], aqk = A[q][k]; A[p][k] = c * apk - s * aqk; A[q][k] = s * apk + c * aqk; }
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { const vkp = V[k][p], vkq = V[k][q]; V[k][p] = c * vkp - s * vkq; V[k][q] = s * vkp + c * vkq; }
    }
  }
  const idx = Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => i).sort((a, b) => A[b][b] - A[a][a]);
  return {vals: idx.map(i => A[i][i]), vecs: idx.map(i => Float64Array.from({length: n}, (_, k) => V[k][i]))};
}
emNet = {
  emNew;
  const N = emN, G = Array.from({length: N}, () => new Float64Array(N));
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) for (let j = i; j < N; j++) { const g = i === j ? 0 : emRandn(); G[i][j] = g; G[j][i] = g; }
  const {vals, vecs} = emEigh(G);
  return {G, lmax: vals[0], vals, vecs, h: Float64Array.from({length: N}, () => emRandn())};
}
emM = {
  const {G, lmax} = emNet, s = emR / lmax;
  return {M: G.map(row => row.map(x => x * s)), vals: emNet.vals.map(x => x * s), vecs: emNet.vecs};
}
emState = {
  emReset;
  const N = emN, {M, vals, vecs} = emM, start = emStart, drive = emDrive;
  const dt = 0.02, tau = 1, T = 20, n = Math.round(T / dt) + 1;
  const h = drive === "const" ? emNet.h : new Float64Array(N);
  let r = new Float64Array(N);
  if (drive === "none") {
    if (start === "random") for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) r[i] = emRandn();
    if (start === "slow" || start === "both") for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) r[i] += vecs[0][i] * Math.sqrt(N);
    if (start === "fast" || start === "both") for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) r[i] += vecs[N - 1][i] * Math.sqrt(N);
    const nrm = Math.sqrt(r.reduce((s, x) => s + x * x, 0)); if (nrm > 0) for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) r[i] *= Math.sqrt(N) / nrm;
  }
  const hist = Array.from({length: N}, () => new Float32Array(n)), amps = Array.from({length: N}, () => new Float32Array(n));
  const a0 = vecs.map(v => v.reduce((s, x, i) => s + x * r[i], 0));
  const record = k => { for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { hist[i][k] = r[i]; let a = 0; for (let j = 0; j < N; j++) a += vecs[i][j] * r[j]; amps[i][k] = a; } };
  record(0);
  let k = 0;
  while (true) {
    if (!viewof emPause.value && k < n - 1) {
      const sig = viewof emNoise.value;
      for (let s = 0; s < 5 && k < n - 1; s++) {
        const rn = new Float64Array(N);
        for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          let inp = h[i]; for (let j = 0; j < N; j++) inp += M[i][j] * r[j];
          rn[i] = r[i] + dt / tau * (-r[i] + inp) + sig * Math.sqrt(dt) * emRandn();
        }
        r = rn; k++; record(k);
      }
    }
    yield {hist, amps, k, t: k * dt, dt, T, a0, vals, h, drive, hvec: vecs.map(v => v.reduce((s, x, i) => s + x * h[i], 0))};
  }
}
emCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 500)
emRaster = DOM.context2d(Math.round(20 / 0.02) + 1, emN, 1)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const st = emState, c = emCanvas, fg = exFg(), W = 760, H = 500, N = emN;
  const {hist, amps, k, dt, T, a0, vals, drive, hvec} = st;
  const orange = "#ff7f0e", blue = "#1f77b4";
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  // panel A: activity raster
  const A = {x0: 60, y0: 14, w: 320, h: 220};
  const n = hist[0].length, img = emRaster.createImageData(n, N);
  let vmax = 1e-6; for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) for (let j = 0; j <= k; j++) vmax = Math.max(vmax, Math.abs(hist[i][j]));
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    const p = 4 * (i * n + j);
    if (j > k) { img.data[p] = 255; img.data[p + 1] = 255; img.data[p + 2] = 255; img.data[p + 3] = 255; continue; }
    const u = Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, hist[i][j] / vmax)), v = Math.sign(u) * Math.sqrt(Math.abs(u));
    const rC = v > 0 ? 255 : Math.round(255 * (1 + v)), bC = v < 0 ? 255 : Math.round(255 * (1 - v)), gC = Math.round(255 * (1 - Math.abs(v)));
    img.data[p] = rC; img.data[p + 1] = gC; img.data[p + 2] = bC; img.data[p + 3] = 255;
  }
  emRaster.putImageData(img, 0, 0);
  c.imageSmoothingEnabled = false; c.drawImage(emRaster.canvas, A.x0, A.y0, A.w, A.h); c.imageSmoothingEnabled = true;
  axisBox(c, A.x0, A.y0, A.w, A.h);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText(`time (units of τ) · t = ${st.t.toFixed(1)}`, A.x0 + A.w / 2, A.y0 + A.h + 24);
  c.fillText("0", A.x0, A.y0 + A.h + 24); c.fillText(T, A.x0 + A.w, A.y0 + A.h + 24);
  c.save(); c.translate(A.x0 - 40, A.y0 + A.h / 2); c.rotate(-Math.PI / 2); c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("neuron", 0, 0); c.restore();
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("1", A.x0 - 8, A.y0 + 10); c.fillText(N, A.x0 - 8, A.y0 + A.h);
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText(`colour: activity ±${vmax.toFixed(1)}, square-root scale`, A.x0, A.y0 + A.h + 46);
  // panel B: mode amplitudes on a log scale
  const B = {x0: 470, y0: 14, w: 270, h: 220}, lo = 1e-3, hi = 20;
  const bx = j => B.x0 + B.w * j / (n - 1), by = a => B.y0 + B.h * (1 - (Math.log10(Math.max(lo, a)) - Math.log10(lo)) / (Math.log10(hi) - Math.log10(lo)));
  axisBox(c, B.x0, B.y0, B.w, B.h);
  c.save(); c.beginPath(); c.rect(B.x0, B.y0, B.w, B.h); c.clip();
  const drawMode = (i, col, lw) => { c.strokeStyle = col; c.lineWidth = lw; c.beginPath(); for (let j = 0; j <= k; j++) j ? c.lineTo(bx(j), by(Math.abs(amps[i][j]))) : c.moveTo(bx(0), by(Math.abs(amps[i][0]))); c.stroke(); };
  c.globalAlpha = 0.35; for (let i = 1; i < N - 1; i++) drawMode(i, "#888", 1); c.globalAlpha = 1;
  drawMode(N - 1, blue, 2); drawMode(0, orange, 2);
  c.setLineDash([5, 4]); c.strokeStyle = fg; c.lineWidth = 1.2;
  for (const i of [0, N - 1]) {
    c.beginPath();
    for (let j = 0; j <= k; j++) {
      const t = j * dt, lam = vals[i], ainf = drive === "const" ? hvec[i] / (1 - lam) : 0;
      const a = ainf + (a0[i] - ainf) * Math.exp(-(1 - lam) * t);
      j ? c.lineTo(bx(j), by(Math.abs(a))) : c.moveTo(bx(0), by(Math.abs(a)));
    }
    c.stroke();
  }
  c.setLineDash([]); c.restore();
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("time (units of τ)", B.x0 + B.w / 2, B.y0 + B.h + 24);
  c.fillText("0", B.x0, B.y0 + B.h + 24); c.fillText(T, B.x0 + B.w, B.y0 + B.h + 24);
  c.textAlign = "right"; for (const v of [1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 1, 10]) c.fillText(v >= 1 ? v : v.toString(), B.x0 - 6, by(v) + 5);
  c.save(); c.translate(B.x0 - 62, B.y0 + B.h / 2); c.rotate(-Math.PI / 2); c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("|mode amplitude|", 0, 0); c.restore();
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillStyle = orange; c.fillText(`slowest mode: λ = ${vals[0].toFixed(2)}, τ₁ = ${(1 / (1 - vals[0])).toFixed(1)} τ`, B.x0 - 60, B.y0 + B.h + 46);
  c.fillStyle = blue; c.fillText(`fastest mode: λ = ${vals[N - 1].toFixed(2)}, τ₄₀ = ${(1 / (1 - vals[N - 1])).toFixed(2)} τ`, B.x0 - 60, B.y0 + B.h + 66);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.fillText("grey: the other modes · dashed: formula", B.x0 - 60, B.y0 + B.h + 86);
  // panel C: eigenvalue spectrum
  const C = {x0: 60, y0: 350, w: 680, h: 110}, emin = -1.1, emax = 1.1;
  const cx = i => C.x0 + C.w * (i + 0.5) / N, cy = v => C.y0 + C.h * (1 - (v - emin) / (emax - emin));
  axisBox(c, C.x0, C.y0, C.w, C.h);
  c.setLineDash([4, 4]); c.strokeStyle = "red"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(C.x0, cy(1)); c.lineTo(C.x0 + C.w, cy(1)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  c.strokeStyle = "#888"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(C.x0, cy(0)); c.lineTo(C.x0 + C.w, cy(0)); c.stroke();
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { c.fillStyle = i === 0 ? orange : i === N - 1 ? blue : "gray"; c.beginPath(); c.arc(cx(i), cy(vals[i]), 4, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); }
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("1", C.x0 - 8, cy(1) + 5); c.fillText("0", C.x0 - 8, cy(0) + 5); c.fillText("−1", C.x0 - 8, cy(-1) + 5);
  c.save(); c.translate(C.x0 - 40, C.y0 + C.h / 2); c.rotate(-Math.PI / 2); c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("eigenvalue", 0, 0); c.restore();
  c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("modes, sorted by eigenvalue", C.x0 + C.w / 2, C.y0 + C.h + 24);
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The top left panel is the activity of all 40 neurons over time, one row per
neuron, red for positive and blue for negative rates, scaled to the largest
value seen so far. The colour scale is a square root, so that small
activity late in the run stays visible. With no input, the activity is set at $t = 0$ by the
initial pattern you chose and then evolves on its own; with constant input
it starts at zero and builds up. Rates below zero are not physical, but a
linear model does not know that, and it is simplest to read the colours as
deviations from a background rate.

The top right panel is the same activity after projecting it onto the
eigenvectors of $\mathbf M$. Each thin grey line is the amplitude of one mode on a
logarithmic axis, so a pure exponential decay is a straight line whose slope
is the decay rate. The slowest mode, the one with the largest eigenvalue, is
orange, and the fastest, with the most negative eigenvalue, is blue. The
dashed lines next to them are the solutions of the one-mode equation above,
computed from the eigenvalue and the initial amplitude alone. They should sit
on top of the simulated lines when the noise is off.

The bottom panel is the spectrum: all 40 eigenvalues sorted from largest to
smallest, with the slow and fast modes coloured to match. The red dashed line
at 1 is the stability limit. The spectral bound $R$ moves the orange point up
and down, and the rest of the spectrum scales with it.

The time axis is in units of $\tau$, the time constant of a single neuron.
The two time constants printed in the top right panel are in the same units.

## Things to try

Start with a random initial pattern and no input at $R = 0.9$. In the raster
the activity fades within a few $\tau$, but not to nothing: a faint pattern
remains and dies away much more slowly. In the mode panel this is obvious.
Every grey line drops steeply, the blue one steepest of all, while the orange
line falls at a tenth of that slope: its time constant is $1/(1 - 0.9) = 10$
times that of a single neuron. After a few $\tau$ the orange mode is all that
is left, and the surviving pattern in the raster is its eigenvector.

Now set the initial activity to the slowest mode alone. The raster shows a
fixed pattern that just fades, and the mode panel is a single straight
orange line, since nothing else was excited. Then pick the fastest mode. Its
pattern alternates sign from neuron to neuron, so the recurrent input to each
neuron opposes its own activity, and it is gone within a $\tau$. The option
with both modes shows the two decays together; after about two $\tau$ the
blue line has dropped below the grey floor and the raster has quietly
switched from one pattern to the other.

Move $R$. At $R = 0.98$ the slowest time constant is $50\,\tau$ and the
orange line is nearly flat; the network has become a memory, holding its
pattern long after the input is gone. At $R = 0.5$ the slow mode lasts only
twice as long as a neuron and the whole spectrum is compressed towards zero.
At $R = 0$ the matrix is zero, there is no recurrence, and all modes decay at
the same rate.

Switch to constant input. Each mode now rises to its steady state $h_i /
(1 - \lambda_i)$, and the dashed lines show the approach. The slow mode is
amplified ten times at $R = 0.9$, so the steady-state pattern of the network
is dominated by its slowest eigenvector almost regardless of what the input
looks like. This is the second thing recurrence does besides lengthening
timescales: it filters the input, keeping the parts that match its slow
modes and suppressing the rest. Click "New random network" to get a
different matrix and a different slow pattern, and notice that the
statements above do not depend on which one you got.

Finally add noise. The grey lines no longer decay but hover at a floor set by
the noise, and the slow mode hovers highest on average, since it integrates
the noise over the longest time. This is the network's spontaneous activity,
and its autocorrelation time is the slow mode's time constant. A network can
be made to look slow without any slow element in it, just by wiring fast
elements into a loop that nearly closes. Measuring such timescales from
recordings is harder than it looks, and much of what I know about it comes
from the groups of [Anna Levina](https://uni-tuebingen.de/en/161236) in
Tübingen and [Tatiana Engel](https://engel-lab.princeton.edu/) at Princeton.
Fitting an exponential to an autocorrelation gives a biased answer for short
recordings, and Zeraati, Engel and Levina (2022) show how to do it properly,
by fitting the data with a mixture of exactly the kind of noisy modes shown
here. In the same spirit, Shi et al. (2023) work out how spatially structured
connections produce several timescales at once, one per spatial frequency,
and Zeraati et al. (2023) find those multiple timescales in recordings from
visual cortex, where the slow one lengthens with attention. The figure above
is the toy version of all three: the spectrum of $\mathbf M$ is the set of
timescales, and $R$ is the knob that attention would turn.

The exercise this page is based on is from the recurrent network chapter of
Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 7). Rajan and Abbott (2006) describe what
the spectrum of a random connection matrix looks like when excitatory and
inhibitory neurons are distinguished, which the symmetric matrix here does
not do.
